## Randomization

- Every causal claim is a comparison between different people (treatment and control).
- Sampling/selection for comparison groups affects how the differences show up.

### Difference between self-selected groups
```{r}
set.seed(6101)
n    <- 2000
conf <- rnorm(n) # Quick and dirty simulation of an occurance in a give population


picked <- ifelse(conf > 0.2, "A", "B") # Self-selection: keener people opt in.
round(mean(conf[picked == "A"]) - mean(conf[picked == "B"]), 3) # compare means between self-selected groups
```


### Difference between randomly selected groups
```{r}

set.seed(6101)
n    <- 2000
conf <- rnorm(n)

imbalance <- replicate(2000, {
  g <- sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE)
  mean(conf[g == "A"]) - mean(conf[g == "B"])
})

hist(imbalance)
hist(imbalance/sd(imbalance))

round(c(mean_imbalance = mean(imbalance),
        sd_imbalance   = sd(imbalance),
        within_95pct   = quantile(abs(imbalance), 0.95)), 4) # 95% of differences in the replication will differ no more than by <x>

```


### Takeaway
- The difference between self selected groups is larger than randomly selected groups.
- Randomization decreases lopsidedness (minimizes differences between groups)

### What Randomization doesn't do
- Does not fix a bad outcome measure
- Does not allow generalization/external validity
- Does not prevent interference (one person's assignment does not affect - interference with - another's outcome).
